A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same multilingual prompting study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original diversity experiments across four LLMs, human evaluation of hallucinated names, mathematical-reasoning evaluations and language-resource analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds Chinese-name frequency analyses and a World Values Survey validation exercise.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same basic and enhanced multilingual/multicultural prompts, separate model queries, GPT-4o-mini back-translation and concatenation. Revised explanations and discussion of alternative aggregation strategies do not establish an algorithm change.

E1.justification: v2 adds ten World Values Survey questions covering social values, religion, politics, environment and security in English, Chinese and Japanese (Appendix A.9, Table 7). The existing Social Chemistry 101, People Diversity, MGSM and language-resource coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain the same monolingual, high-temperature, random-persona, requesting-diversity and step-by-step-recall comparisons, including their task-specific omissions. New Table 8 redisplays the existing comparator set; the WVS exercise adds no comparison method.

E3.justification: Appendix A.9 introduces a ten-question, three-language validation protocol, selecting questions partly because preliminary answers already differed across languages. Existing experiments retain their prompts, model configurations, response counts, entropy metrics and human-annotation design.

E4.justification: v2 adds a targeted analysis of Chinese-name concentration under basic versus enhanced prompts (Section 4.3), a concrete profession-name hallucination example (Section 5), and the WVS validation exercise. Existing prompt-variation, language-resource and instruction-following analyses remain.

E5.justification: The significance markers in Table 1 and error bars in Figure 3 and the appendix diversity plots are retained. v2 adds no repeated-run counts, seed information or uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and 4–6 retain their numerical results. v2 newly reports disagreement across languages for 9/10 selected WVS questions and Chinese-name counts, including 547 versus 427 for enhanced versus basic GPT-4o prompts, from 1,050 names each. The hallucination error rates restate v1's validity counts, while Table 8 largely expresses existing scores as baseline-relative ratios.

T1.justification: The entropy definitions, finite-sample normalization bounds and Sentence-BERT perspective-diversity formulation in Appendices A.3–A.4 are retained. The rewritten reason-entropy expression is algebraically equivalent; no substantive assumptions, derivations or proofs change.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: multilingual prompting improves diversity over existing approaches, matching language with cultural cues reduces hallucination, and benefits vary with language resources and model size.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 newly explains stronger cultural cues as potentially narrowing demographic coverage, distinguishing basic prompts for broad diversity from enhanced prompts for culturally specific responses. Appendix A.10 acknowledges computational overhead and argues when it may be worthwhile. Existing aggregation and translation limitations remain.

D1.justification: Section 3 replaces v1's promise to release code pending acceptance with a concrete repository link described as available. Existing prompt templates, translation-model disclosure and human-study procedures are substantially unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds Chatterji et al. (2025) on ChatGPT usage and Zhang et al. (2024) on fairness implications of machine unlearning. The principal positioning relative to persona prompting, sampling methods and language-specific knowledge remains unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 copyedits and clarifies several introductory, methodological and baseline passages, divides Section 4's setup into dataset/metrics and baseline/performance subsections, and adds an appendix roadmap and acknowledgments. The overall narrative and most existing appendix prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 replaces the roommate example with family reunions and adds translations; Figure 2 is redrawn. New Figure 4 visualizes existing hallucination outcomes, and Tables 7–8 display WVS responses and relative scores. Later displays are relocated or renumbered within the retained two-column layout.

improvement.justification: v2 improves accessibility and interpretation through clearer organization, documented code access and the new analysis of basic versus enhanced prompting. These gains are limited: WVS questions were selected partly for observed language differences, and the cost discussion supplies no cost measurements. New Table 8 also reports a 1.23x enhanced-multicultural demographic ratio although Table 1 implies 0.378/0.315 = 1.20x. These localized weaknesses temper the documentation and explanatory improvements; the core empirical evidence remains unchanged.
